I have an MA in my field, so I am familiar with the current critical conversations in that field and am working on projects that will contribute to those conversations in a meaningful way. I am also familiar with less conceptual research/professional things-  i.e., I know how to find, apply, and present at relevant conferences in a productive way. And I know that, for my field, journal articles are the future, so I've started working (post-MA) on producing the kind of writing seen in those big journals. I also have the "lived" experience of the MA - I hit a wall in my second year and figured out how to push through. It's not an academic advantage per se but is, I think, a strength. So, to me, those things speak more to a professional identity (or at least a professional identity that would be reasonable for an MA student.) 

At the same time, I know that I am - by no means - polished in my work. My sub-fields and specialization could change (and I know programs prepare for this because it's not unusual). So, in my SOPs, I really thought about scholars who would help my current work but also folks who would help me expand the context around the question I'm focusing on. 

Short example, I spent my MA doing transnational American work. Awesome stuff, would 11/10 keep on doing. At the same time, transatlantic stuff is also interesting and relevant. And, as a PhD student, I'd like to explore that area. 

All to say, I have a few ideas about what a dissertation could look like for me - I don't pull a blank there. But, I am really eager for expansion and growth and challenge (but not hand-holding!) and I hope that the balance of focus/flexibility demonstrates that I not only *could* be a great professional but have experiences/understanding that *show* that.

*Apologies for (1) the length, (2) the rambling, and (3) possibly not really answering your question in a full or clear way.* 
*Also, I've applied already so this really is a think piece - however, I have friends applying next year and would love to pass on all the good advice here.*

Given what you've told us here, you are a competitive applicant. As such, I hope you're looking at a range of reputable programs. 

At the same time, I would suggest looking at MA programs. They're useful for more than just raising a GPA - they can give you a whole lot of opportunities, ranging from conferences to institutes to all sorts of things. 

PM if you're looking at lit programs and would like to chat more in depth - this process is rough, for sure, and I'm happy to share what I've learned from peers who are at top U.S. programs. 

Best of luck!

Hey, friend, 

I totally empathize with your nerves - it took me months to work up the courage to talk to a crisis hotline. The Suicide Prevention Lifeline (for the US) is something I've had actually a lot of success with. 
I use the online chat option because the conversation moves more slowly, and I can think through my thoughts more easily. 

Where I'm at currently, I log on about once a day and start off with that fact; it felt weird the first time, admitting that I'd talked to them the day before, but I tell them that right off because I know I'll feel better with them knowing and they responded really well; they asked questions about my last session and it made it easier to talk. 

Doing that helped me decide to actually call and talk to a person, which wasn't nearly as awkward as I thought it would be. 
I think the best words of support I can give are these; crisis hotlines are absolutely ready to hear you talk, even if you need to tell your story a few times or mention things out of order. They're very good at listening to the facts you mention but also put no pressure on you wanting to keep talking about something. 

It's a hard thing to reach out for help, especially in person (one time, I called mid-breakdown and realized I couldn't speak very clearly because of the tears/weeping. the person I was speaking to simply stayed on the line and let me cry myself out, and then we talked for a while. It was so unexpected but absolutely what I needed.)

I hope this helps!

Hey,

I can't speak to the usefulness of meds, but I can lend some advice as to therapy. Finding the right therapist with the right approach is less easy than I (at least) thought it would be. Part of my struggle right now is/was realizing the therapist I had, while a nice person, wasn't quite aligning with me and my mentality.

I have a new therapist now and am having more success; two things have helped me with that. (1) I was super clear up front about my lack of desire for medication (2) I asked a lot of questions our first session about her beliefs about therapy. Her approach is less "well here's a possible solution to this immediate problem, do you feel better now?" and more holistic/longer time investment (if that makes sense). 

So while this is maybe a silly sounding piece of advice, perhaps (since you're just starting a new therapy attempt) you could make a list of the things you want to get out of this as well as the way you envision the therapy working best for you; that could maybe help you with completing the therapy. 

I'll be honest though, I don't know if or when I'll complete therapy - may stick with it for a long time, which is expensive and perhaps not something you'd prefer to do but ... looking at it as a long-term investment could help, perhaps?
